speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The first category of amendments involves changes to processes related to election candidates.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The second category improves the management of contingencies during an election.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The third and final category deals with other election processes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Clause 4 amends section 28 to simplify the computation of election deposits.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The clause also deletes the reference to cash payment and, in its place, provides the option for candidates to pay the election deposit by electronic fund transfer or in such other form or manner as the Returning Officer allows.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The other methods of payment currently provided in the Act by bank draft or certified cheque will continue to be available.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: To facilitate smooth and orderly conduct of nomination proceedings, clause 6 amends section 31 to provide that a person seeking to be a candidate in an election may be refused entry to the place of nomination unless the aspiring candidate satisfies the requirements set out in the new section 31(2).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These requirements are that the aspiring candidate must have a political donation certificate issued under section 18(4) of the Political Donations Act and be accompanied by at least six other individuals, namely, his proposer, seconder and at least four assentors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In the case of a Group Representation Constituency, additional requirements apply, including that at least one member in the group must also have a certificate from either the Malay Community Committee or the Indian and other Minority Communities Committee.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These requirements are also necessary for successful nomination.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: With the proposed changes, election officials can focus on processing the nomination papers of those who are serious about meeting the requirements for nomination.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The next set of amendments deals with the returns on election expenses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We will streamline and simplify the submission of returns on election expenses without diluting accountability.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The clause also empowers the Returning Officer to require, during this one-year period, the candidate or the election agent, or both of them, to furnish any supporting document or any other information relating to the return.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Any contravention of the requirements of the new section 75A constitutes an illegal practice.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: To protect personal data, clause 24 amends section 75 to require the Returning Officer to redact certain personal details when the returns and statements on election expenses are open for public inspection.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Addresses and contact numbers will be completely redacted.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: However, for accountability, the names of candidates, election agents and donors will continue to be reflected in full with their identity card numbers partially redacted.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Next, I will discuss the proposed amendments to section 83.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Section 83 of the Parliamentary Elections Act currently prohibits certain classes of people, such as foreigners, from taking part in any election activity and also requires the persons conducting election activities for a candidate to be authorised to do so by the candidate or his election agent.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Section 83 currently defines "election activity" as including an "activity which is done for the purpose of promoting or procuring the election of a candidate at any election".

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Clause 26 amends the definition of "election activity" mainly to elaborate that an activity which is done to prejudice the electoral prospects of other political parties or candidates is also election activity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill does not make any changes to the substantive rules in section 83 on election activity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill spells out various procedures to strengthen the current provisions to manage various types of contingencies, such as a riot, fire or flood, which may occur during nomination, polling or counting proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: I will now take Members through the key changes being proposed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Clause 17 inserts a new section 56BA to enable the Returning Officer to deal with contingencies affecting the conduct of nomination proceedings on the day of nomination.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: If a contingency arises before the start of nomination proceedings on nomination day, the new section 56BA provides the Returning Officer with the powers to change the hours of the nomination proceedings, change the place of nomination, or to do both, or abandon nomination proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: If the Returning Officer decides to change the hours of nomination proceedings, the new hours must enable the nomination proceedings to start and conclude within the same day.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: If a contingency arises during the nomination proceedings, the new section 56BA(3) provides the Returning Officer with the powers to suspend the nomination proceedings for a period of time and continue with the nomination proceedings at the end of the period at the same nomination place or at a different place on the same date, or abandon the nomination proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Should there be a need to conduct nomination proceedings on another day, the President will issue a fresh writ stating the new date for nomination as provided under existing law.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Similarly, for polling and counting proceedings, clauses 18, 20 and 21 amend sections 56C, 56E and 56F respectively to empower the Returning Officer to suspend the proceedings for up to two hours to assess the situation and decide on the course of action to be taken.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We will also be replicating various changes to deal with contingencies, which we made to the Presidential Elections Act last year.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These are covered in clause 13, which amends section 49A to empower the Returning Officer to extend the time taken for sealed ballot boxes from overseas polling stations to reach Singapore; clause 19 which inserts new sections 56DA and 56DB to spell out the procedures to be taken when marked local ballot papers are lost or destroyed when they are being transported after the close of polls to counting places and when marked overseas ballot papers are lost or destroyed when they are being transported from overseas polling stations to the counting place in Singapore; and clause 12, which amends section 48A to remove the current requirement for the Returning Officer to inform candidates or their election agents in writing as to the places where the votes will be counted or the postponement of counting due to certain contingencies described in that section.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Instead, the Returning Officer will publish the information in the Government Gazette.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The third category of amendments deals with other election processes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Clause 2 amends section 9 to remove the requirement for the Registration Officer to publish in the Government Gazette the polling districts within an electoral division.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Instead, the Registration Officer will publish maps or other images of the polling districts on the Elections Department's website.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This will make it easier for members of public to view the polling districts compared to the current method of using text, such as road names, to describe polling districts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Registration Officer will continue to publish in the Government Gazette a notice when an electoral division is subdivided into polling districts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The notice will provide details of the website and the physical locations where the maps can be inspected by the public.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The clause improves administrative efficiency in processing the claims specified in a new section 11(9B).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For other types of claims, the Registration Officer will continue to hold a public inquiry before deciding whether to accept or reject such claims.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Claimants whose claims are rejected without an inquiry have a right to appeal to the Revising Officer, appointed by the Minister, under the current section 12.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Clause 8 amends section 39 to empower the Minister to prescribe in regulations the method for computing the number of polling agents for each candidate or a group of candidates who may enter a polling station.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This will enable the number of polling agents in a polling station to be made proportionate to the number of voters allotted to the polling station instead of the current pegging of polling agents to the number of polling places in the polling station.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This amendment gives flexibility to the Elections Department to design polling stations for efficient operation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: To illustrate, Elections Department plans to introduce electronic voter registration or e-registration.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This will result in a faster registration process for voters.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: With a faster registration process, the same number of voters in a polling station can be served by fewer polling places.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: To ensure an adequate number of polling agents for each polling station despite fewer polling places in the polling station, we propose to peg the number of polling agents to the number of voters in the polling station.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The amendment Bill also replicates relevant changes made to the Presidential Elections Act last year through the amendments in clauses 7, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15 and 28(n).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These relate to the notices to voters on voting procedures placed outside polling stations, the design of the ballot paper, recounting of votes, and election advertising.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: All these changes were elaborated during the amendments to the Presidential Elections Act last year and I will not repeat them today.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Currently, the number of NCMPs to be declared is nine, minus the total number of elected Opposition Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I was flabbergasted and perplexed at the same time on how the ARO could have arrived at such a conclusion.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The said voter could easily be an elderly person who, for some reason, could not imprint a more forceful mark on that ballot paper but that did not mean his or her intention was not clear in any way.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I have also seen ballot papers with a tick and a diagonal line drawn across it, well within the demarcated box for the preferred candidate, being marked for rejection.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The reason, a tick means "yes" but the diagonal line across it forms an "X", which means "no".

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, yes and no at the same time, the intention of the voter was not clear.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Yet, I have seen an "X" marked on the party logo area counted as valid.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I have also witnessed symbols and expletives in the demarcated box of a ballot paper counted as valid as well.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, I am looking at potentially six different interpretations of what constitutes a valid vote, just in one counting centre alone.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: How can we call ourselves a developed country when we cannot even define, in simple terms and without ambiguity, what is a valid vote?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, while this amendment Bill seeks to issue clearer guidelines on what the Returning Officers and their assistants should look for in a ballot paper when determining the intention of the voter, I wish to seek some clarifications from the Minister on some of the proposed changes.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am sure many of us in this House would have come across ballot papers with the voter’s mark imprinted outside the area demarcated for that purpose.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I believe the intentions of these voters were in no way unclear.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: However, such votes would be deemed invalid under the proposed amendment to section 42 of the Parliamentary Elections Act.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We are an ageing society and we will see more and more elderly voters in time to come.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I have utmost respect for these voters who, despite their advanced age or disability, are determined to play a role in shaping our democracy, come what may.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It would be sad to know that their effort and passion could be in vain with the proposed amendment.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I seek more information from the Minister to address this concern.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Separately, I hope the Elections Department could also look into designing a ballot paper with a larger area demarcated for the voters to mark with greater ease.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Second, clause 15, which amends section 50 of the principal Act, introduces a new sub-section (2A) to instruct the Returning Officer, when determining whether a mark made on a ballot paper clearly indicates the voter’s intention to vote for the candidate or group of candidates, to disregard any mark that is not made within the area demarcated on the ballot paper for that purpose.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I wish to ask the Minister, does that mean that as long as a voter’s mark is made within the area demarcated on the ballot paper for that purpose, a voter is allowed to exercise his artistic licence elsewhere on the ballot paper and it would still be counted as a valid vote, since the Returning Officer must disregard other mark found on the ballot paper as directed under this new amendment?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If a voter were to cross out the name of a particular candidate with words like “clown”, "my hero" or "Mr Bean", and then proceed to put an “X” in the area demarcated on the ballot paper for that purpose, would the Returning Officer be compelled to treat it as a valid vote under this proposed amendment to section 50 of the Parliamentary Elections Act?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I hope the Minister can provide more clarity on this amendment, else it will only cause more confusion.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Voting is a serious act of civic responsibility.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I believe we should not allow the ballot paper to be marked in any other way other than prescribed under the Act.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: There should be no other mark other than the mark left by the voter in the area demarcated on the ballot paper for that purpose.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Returning Officers should not be tasked to disregard any other mark found on the ballot paper but to designate such ballot as invalid, as outright invalid.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Beyond showing voters where to mark on a ballot paper, the Elections Department should also educate voters on what will invalidate their votes.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: At this juncture, I wish to reiterate the Workers' Party’s stand on the NCMP scheme.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not oppose the Bill and I concur with the various points made by my colleague Mr Png Eng Huat on the Bill, which I shall not repeat here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will pose several questions and request for clarification.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would he or she, for example, access the relevant Government database for personal information and, if so, what safeguards are there against errors, such as laxity in updating such databases?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Previously, the Act prescribed what information would be reflected in such notices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, part of the old section 37 read, and I quote, "37(1): Outside each polling station, there shall be affixed, in a conspicuous place, by the Presiding Officer, before the commencement of the poll, a notice showing the name of each candidate in English, Malay, Chinese and Tamil, and a symbol allotted to the candidate under section 34.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And two, the names of the candidates shall be arranged alphabetically in English, in the order of their surnames and, if there are two or more candidates with the same surname, of their other names." I would like to ask what is the reason for removing these prescriptions and providing the Minister with broad latitude to determine the content of these notices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What guidelines or rules will the Minister be bound by making such a determination.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, clause 8 amends section 39 to empower the Minister to prescribe the method for computing the number of polling agents for each candidate or groups of candidates who may enter a polling station.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason given is to allow the Minister to ensure that the permitted number of polling agents is proportionate to the number of voters allotted to that station.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to ask if the legislative intent here is for the Minister to be able to ensure that the ratio of polling agents to voters is more or less similar across polling stations nationwide and in line with recent nationwide averages which is clearly desirable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or is the intent that the Minister should be able to exercise this discretion by varying the average nationwide ratio of polling agents to voters significantly away from the recent averages, either by increasing or decreasing the ratio?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rather, the information will be published in the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would it not be possible to automate the broadcast of a simple email or text message to election agents and all candidates upon new information being published in the Gazette?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members are advised to keep to the contents of the debate.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The NCMP scheme is not relevant to this debate.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The parts of section 37 which are to be removed include sub-sections (1), (2), (3), (4), (5) and (6).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They list out basic information, such as names of candidates in four different languages to be placed in a notice outside the station with their respective symbols, such names to be listed alphabetically, and so on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The proposed new section 37(2) states, for example, at (a) that the notice must contain such information presented in such form or manner, as may be prescribed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And what are the reasons for the proposed changes to section 37?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And was there any particular incident which has given rise to the proposed changes?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 19 provides for a new section 56DA and 56DB after the existing section 56D.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Section 56DA(7) and (8) and 56DB(1)(a)(b) relates to the postponement and abandonment of polling.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The new provision sets out the considerations and mechanism for decision-making by the Returning Officer in respect of different scenarios.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why is the Government suddenly concerned about these scenarios provided for in the new provisions?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are the proposed amendments due to any particular incident which happened in recent years?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And will the basis for a decision be recorded with sufficient details and made available to any such claimant upon demand?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must always strive to have a clear and unequivocal set of rules for the Returning Officers (ROs) to make the right determination with minimal chances of any dispute by any candidate and with good sense and bereft of any perverse or absurd outcome.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, such rules must ensure, and I am going to give an extreme example, that expletives written in the demarcated box of one candidate cannot sensibly be regarded as a vote for that candidate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, I hope to confine my remarks to non-partisan issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The elections process must give the Government of the day a clear mandate to govern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this Bill does reflect the Government's intent to ensure elections in Singapore are efficient, future-proof and conducted with integrity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we should also think beyond the next general election.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: How will future politicians use, or abuse, these laws, and how will our history as a democracy be shaped by this Bill?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, let me start with the problem of history.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But it may unintentionally harm the historical record of changes in our electoral divisions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Gazette is a permanent part of our history and cannot be readily altered or destroyed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But materials that you publish online have little permanence – Internet links break, websites go down, documents can be altered or deleted without notice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot even predict whether the Internet will exist in the form we are used to today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us grew up using microfilm readers for research.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our children do not; our grandchildren almost certainly would not even know what microfilm is.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But printed work has somehow stood the test of time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Scholars will use the Gazette in the future to research how our electoral divisions changed, how that affects representation, how that affects outcomes in society and the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is a paper, "The Political Economy of Housing Prices", published in the Journal of Housing Economics in 2010 by Eddie Sue and Wong Wei-Kang at the National University of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This paper studies how electoral boundaries affect housing prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I leave it to Members to make guesses as to whether Government or Opposition wards enjoy higher housing prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I hope this will encourage Members to read more academic papers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In an article dated 24 July 2015, The Straits Times calculated that one in five voters were affected by redistricting ahead of the 2015 General Election (GE), and nearly one in three voters were affected by the 2011 GE redistricting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, a change that is so consequential should form a future-proof part of our historical record.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Before I move to the second issue, that of re-polling in the event of a lost or destroyed ballot box, l realise a similar debate took place during the Presidential Elections (Amendment) Bill in 2017.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are some differences, though, so I do beg Members' indulgence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think this problem of clause 19 is how do we minimise the political costs and risks associated with an election.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If the margin of victory is within that number of uncounted votes, including overseas electors, then, a new poll must be conducted for that station.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The identity of the Government may well hang in the balance of that one polling station.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, let us ask: how likely is it that an election will require re-polling, under the amendment Bill?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Elections Department informs me there were 832 polling stations in the 2015 GE, and there were about 2.46 million eligible voters, and there are typically between two and four ballot boxes in each polling station.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That is an average of 3,000 voters in each polling station.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Suppose that by some disaster, one ballot box is lost from every single electoral division.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: How many re-polls would we have to conduct?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Obviously, SMCs are more likely to require re-polling because the margin of victory is more likely to be within the number of votes in one polling station.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A polling station, on average, will contain 11.5% of the electorate for an SMC, and about 2.4% of the electorate for a GRC.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We are accustomed, of course, to the present Government winning elections by large margins.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This may not be so in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As margins become tighter, the risk of a re-polling event does rise if a ballot box is lost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Now, Sir, how can we improve on this?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The question is whether the lost ballot box represents a random sample of the votes cast at the affected polling station.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: After all, votes are generally cast into a ballot box in no particular order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Polling procedures can further improve on this by ensuring that voters who arrive as groups and who may vote similarly, such as families, are to split their ballots between the boxes randomly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If the votes contained within one ballot box are actually missing at random, there is no issue in counting the remaining votes from the affected polling station.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The procedures described in the Bill can apply in the event that the margin of victory still remains smaller than the missing votes from that particular ballot box.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I understand this clause was adapted from the Presidential Elections (Amendment) Bill in 2017.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But, you see, Mr Speaker, these issues are unlikely to affect the Presidential Election because a polling station contains less than 0.2% of the vote in a Presidential Election.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is a much larger issue in a Parliamentary Election.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And, of course, this may create the appearance of a conflict of interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The same applies, of course, to the Parliamentary Elections Act, where section 102 reserves the power to the Minister to make regulations regarding the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think that we have no issue with this during the term of Government because the voters have clearly given their mandate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But there is this particular issue arising between the time when Parliament is dissolved and until when the new Parliament first sits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am not criticising the integrity of the Government or of Members here today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But this is a law for the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We would hope that future generations would act with integrity, we hope they would act exactly as we would.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But should we write laws that depend at critical moments on future officeholders acting only in the best interests of the country?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I share with this Government the view that our laws should be written in the long-term interest of the country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: On balance, I expect the Bill will achieve that objective, but I hope the Government will be able to address some of these concerns.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the same vein, and I am sure the other Members of the House would agree, we look forward to the contributions from the other Nominated Members of Parliament who have just been sworn in and will make their speeches in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The overriding aim is, of course, to uphold the integrity of the process, and make sure that public confidence in the election process is always high.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And I use the word "process" in its widest sense, from the processes involving the Electoral Register to the processes involving Nomination, conduct of elections and, of course, elections expenses as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Presumably, it is part of the Government's push to make Singapore go cashless.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This lies in contrast with section 10(3) of the Presidential Elections Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Members would note that the Presidential Elections Act was revised just last year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do appreciate the Government's push to convert our society to a cashless one.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I half suspect that the hon Minister Ong Ye Kung, who is in charge of this initiative, may even advocate payment using PayNow.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At this point, though, a significant part of our society still uses cash.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Why is it necessary in these circumstances to remove deposits by legal tender?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it be better not to hurry this until our society has really become cash-free, which is not the case now?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With reference to the usage of certified cheques, how is this mode impacted by the Government intent that our society stops using cheques by 2025?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would the Elections Department anticipate making further changes to this payment mode then?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also note that there is no process outline on how the deposit would be returned.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, if you are pushing for cashless transactions, then perhaps we should provide for end-to-end such that the deposits may be contemplated to be returned to a specified account provided by the candidates via the electronic funds transfer system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, in the last Elections, I had the chance to invoke the previous process as a candidate for Aljunied GRC when the candidates had to decide whether a recount was necessary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And Mr Speaker, Sir, it was almost like an episode from "The Amazing Race" because we had to make our way from the assembly area to the principal counting centre.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We had to drive there and, through the process, we were not sure whether we would be too late to meet the Returning Officer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And finally, when we met the Returning Officer, we asked for a recount.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Then, he took out a paper and read from the script, agreeing to our request.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, there were quite a lot of moving parts in the old process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This process is much better because the rationale behind the recounting is solely to ensure the accuracy of the vote count, given the close margins.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, it makes sense for the Returning Officer to be reposed with the power to initiate the process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The final point, Mr Speaker, Sir, is on Parliamentary expenses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The current system, in my respectful view, has good accountability.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There can be public access to the bills and receipts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They can check whether the election expenses regulations have been observed by looking at the source documents and not just the statements.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If there is any discrepancy or shortcoming, then there is the ability to deal with it, then and there, close to the holding of the elections.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, this perhaps may loosen the form of accountability and may impact on the integrity of the process.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This amendment is unpalatable to many voters who strongly believe that every vote is sacred.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Why should all the votes at the affected polling station be nullified due to a single loss, damaged or tampered box?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a recommendation which a number of constituents are uncomfortable with and find difficult to accept.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Why can we not proceed with the counting of the votes from the unaffected, sealed ballot boxes?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I think that a re-poll of the affected electoral division does not necessarily ensure a fair and equitable election.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is as good as holding a by-election, especially when the national results have already been announced.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What were the measures taken to ensure the transparent and indisputable transfer of ballot boxes from polling stations to counting centres?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the doubts raised was the possibility of ballot boxes being replaced during transfers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to ask for details about how ballot boxes from overseas are organised.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, I would like to ask whether the Elections Department can provide the ballot paper sample which uses black as the base colour.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My concern is that it may affect voters' ability to identify the candidates or the party logos on the ballot papers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Elderly voters may have difficulties reading the ballot papers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Has a consultation been done with different age groups about the design of the ballot paper to ensure clarity of design and readability?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, how would the Elections Department ensure that the Assistant Returning Officers or polling staff provide indisputable guidance to voters at polling stations?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Had there been reports or complaints made in past elections, such as those about assistants prompting voters to tick for certain candidates while addressing their queries at the polling stations?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will further strengthen the efforts by the Government to ensure the building of an inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The deposit should preferably be set at a level that will not discriminate against those who have less wealth but have the qualities and willingness to serve.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I welcome the use of maps to show the boundaries to enable the electorate to know their constituencies prior to the GE.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will provide greater ease of viewing and clarity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These can be grouped into three broad sets of issues.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The first set of issues has to do with the provisions related to election candidates.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second set of issues relates to management of contingencies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The third set of issues has some unrelated issues which the Speaker has reminded us that are not relevant to this Bill, but nevertheless, I will make a few short remarks, in particular, on the NCMP scheme.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh suggested reducing the election deposit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The purpose of the election deposit is to ensure that only those who are serious in contesting in the elections step forward.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I agree with him that we should not set the amount so high that it becomes a barrier to entry.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we also need to strike a balance.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And under the law, candidates who contest and gather more than one-eighth of the votes will have their election deposits returned to them after the election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Murali Pillai suggested that we continue to allow cash payment of election deposits.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The amendments will increase the options, not decrease the options in the mode of payment.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are encouraging candidates to use electronic funds transfer to make it more convenient for aspiring candidates so that they no longer need to withdraw cash or visit a bank to purchase a bank draft and go to the Accountant-General’s Department to make the payment.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Elections Department will also return the election deposits using electronic funds transfer, and it is as per the current process, the candidate has the choice to which method of refund that they would like to use.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As for cash, this is something the Returning Officer may allow when there are technical issues with the electronic funds transfer system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we have increased the number of choices, rather than narrow it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh also suggested automating nomination forms.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Elections Department is looking into expanding its range of e-Services to candidates and election agents, and we will consider Mr Gan’s suggestion as part of their study.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Murali Pillai spoke about possible unintended consequences from removing the need for candidates to submit supporting documents, such as bills and receipts, in their returns on election expenses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As there have not been any issues with these returns in the past, we propose to remove the need to submit these supporting documents to improve administration efficiency.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we are only doing away with supporting documents.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The rest of the submissions are still required.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Candidates are also required to keep these supporting documents for a period of one year, and the Returning Officer may require these documents for checks, where needed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, the candidates still need to submit the necessary declarations and it is just that the supporting documents need not come with it, unless there is a public enquiry, a public interest in this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Leon Perera and Mr Dennis Tan asked why some of the issues are moved out of the Act.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is because, in our review, we made a distinction between operational matters which can be done in the subsidiary legislation, and the legislative matters which are required in the Act.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we are not removing the clauses that the Members have mentioned, but we are shifting them into the subsidiary legislation, so that we simplify the Act itself.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the issue of the number of polling agents required, we have simplified this so that it is according to the number of voters, rather than the number of polling places.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There is no intention to decrease or increase the number of polling agents overall, but this will allow us to better match the number of polling agents with the number of voters, and it would be an easier way for everyone to understand the processes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The third issue raised by Mr Leon Perera is the issue of notifications.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It will be done simultaneously via the Gazette and also available on the Elections Department website, so that it is easily available for everyone to check when there is an announcement to be made by Elections Department.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Next, let me touch on the management of contingencies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira spoke about the proposed procedures should a ballot box be lost or destroyed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All voters assigned to the affected polling station will then have to re-cast their votes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is because when voters drop their ballot papers into the ballot boxes in any polling station, they have a choice.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It will not be possible for us to ascertain which voters cast their votes in the affected ballot box.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is why it goes by the polling station, rather than the individual voter.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And this will only be done if, as I have explained, it affects the polling results for the electoral division.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The procedure we are proposing is not new.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira suggested to minimise the need for fresh polls by changing the polling procedures in the polling station.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There is a downside to that because the current procedure is designed to allow voters to drop their ballot paper into any ballot box, so that voters can be assured of voting secrecy, as an added check.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, this has served us well, and I think we will continue this current arrangement.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are also contingency provisions and procedures that we want to put in place.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira observed that if there were lost or damaged ballot boxes in an SMC, chances would be higher for a fresh poll to be conducted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Consequently, there was no instance of re-polling as a result of loss or destruction of ballot boxes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And, if, indeed, ballot boxes get lost or damaged, the amendment in today’s Bill would lay out clearly in the law the steps to take to deal with such a scenario to ensure the integrity of the election process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members have also asked has there been any event that triggered us to review the current existing procedures.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The answer is that this has always been part of our ongoing work in the Elections Department to make sure that our processes are kept afresh.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As Assoc Prof Walter Theseira said, we need to think long term, we need to anticipate what may happen even though it may not have happened yet.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The provision in section 56DA(8) is to provide the Minister with the powers to prescribe other operational details in the regulations, if required, such as the notice to be placed outside the polling station.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In response to Member Mr Dennis Tan, we are thinking ahead of possible contingencies, rather than being triggered by any recent or past occurrence.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Dennis Tan also asked for the grounds of rejection.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Registration Officer will reply to the claimant, and if the claimant so chooses, he or she may make public the reasons for the rejection.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, it will not be the Registration Officer who makes public the reasons for the rejection, but it is made available to the claimant, and he or she can make the necessary public announcement if they so choose to.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will now touch on other points raised by Members.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the design of the ballot paper, we share Mr Png Eng Huat’s and Mr Gan Thiam Poh's concern for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And this is, indeed, the reason why we have recently refreshed our polling paper design.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The use of black as the base colour was introduced at GE2015 to help focus voters’ attention on the box to mark their voting choice.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The background for the parts containing the candidate’s photograph and symbol remain white, so that these parts are clearly visible, and in clear contrast to the voters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Elections Department took in the views of voters of different age groups when coming up with the new ballot paper design.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Png Eng Huat asked about the adjudication process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have very clear adjudication rules and process set up, and the Elections Department routinely conducts training for all the Assistant Returning Officers (AROs), the Group Assistant Returning Officers (GAROs), so that they can do their job professionally.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we should also put in context, such as how many of these votes actually go into adjudication.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Actually, the answer is very few, but notwithstanding that it is very few that really require adjudication, we constantly make sure that training of our AROs and GAROs are all done systematically and professionally.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And they are not partisan to any particular party.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They will adjudicate based on their professional judgement on how best this is to be done.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Election officers are trained to adjudicate based on whether the voters' choice is clear, according to the law.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Now, with the amendment to only consider markings in the demarcated area of the ballot paper, we will remind voters to mark their choices with an "X" for the candidate, or, in the case of a GRC, the group of candidates they are voting for, in the demarcated area of the ballot paper.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And Mr Png Eng Huat may like to help us to remind voters to mark the "X" in the demarcated area, rather than to exercise their artistic talent in the polling station.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For transparency, the process is open to observation by candidates and their agents.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When sealed ballot boxes are transported from polling stations to counting centres, candidates and their polling agents may also board the buses to observe the process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They are then transported from the Supreme Court to the counting place to be counted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Election officials are not allowed to influence voters on who to vote for.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Each voter decides for himself who to vote for.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Where election officials have to communicate with voters, for example, in the case of visually handicapped voters, to guide them on using the stencil, they do so in an audible voice so that candidates, agents and other election officials around them can hear the conversation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked if the move to an online-only publication of polling districts will adversely affect historical records and, hence, future research.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members of the public can also continue to view electoral boundaries interactively using the Singapore Land Authority (SLA) OneMap.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They can also inspect or purchase these maps in hardcopy at the offices of SLA and the Elections Department.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have gone through this debate previously in this House.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We had also debated this during the Constitutional amendments.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the Workers' Party feels that it is not in its Party's manifesto or beliefs to support the NCMP scheme, then we have two choices in front of us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One, it is for the Workers' Party candidates, during elections to publicly declare that he or she will not take up the NCMP seat even if offered.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second option is for the Workers' Party to impose a rule on all its Members to not take up an NCMP seat even if it is offered and this will be the Workers' Party's guideline.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think with these two options, the Workers' Party can take its pick on what it wants to do.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But it would be rather disingenuous to say that we oppose the NCMP scheme and, at the same time, to take up the NCMP seats.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I leave it to the Workers' Party on the choice that it wants to make going forward, and I am sure that enlightened Singaporeans will understand why and what the Workers' Party wants to do.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They are part of the continuous improvements to strengthen election administration and to improve services to voters and candidates.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With that, Mr Speaker, Sir, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I urge all Members to give your support to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: On the response of the hon Minister in relation to the payment of deposit, Members of the House will recall that the hon Minister said that in legal tender is in addition to the other modes prescribed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, may I seek a clarification from the Minister, is the hon Minister relying on the catch-all provision at the end that the Returning Officer would allow legal tender as well?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: If that is so, then my concerns will be addressed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Actually, my clarification is on the similar point that Mr Murali Pillai raised.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Because I think earlier, the Minister in his round-up speech, said that the Returning Officer could allow the election deposit to be paid in cash if, for example, the electronic transfer failed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, is that the only circumstance when cash would be accepted, meaning that there were some problems with the Internet or electronic transfer?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Because it does seem to set another barrier for candidates who may be raising money up to the very last minute and may not be able to do the funds electronically.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Or if you are talking about last-minute crowd-sourcing, so if there are extenuating circumstances, I think candidates can let the Returning Officers know and they will exercise the discretion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Meaning that actually the failure of the electronic transfers is not a prerequisite, that means to say, there could be other circumstances why they could not do the electronic transfer?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Png Eng Huat, is your question pertaining to the NCMP?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Would the Minister, in the interest of transparency, make the adjudication process training public, so that at least we, as candidates, would know how AROs adjudicate such invalid votes?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I do not think that there is anything secret about it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We train thousands and thousands of public officials on how to do it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I think the Elections Department would be happy to share with Mr Png Eng Huat how we train our officers.
